questions.question: What is the primary goal of cyber security?
options: To protect systems, networks, and data from digital attacks
To make sure everyone has the fastest internet speed possible
To help people find information faster on search engines
To fix broken hardware like computer screens and keyboards
questions.explanation: Cyber security is the practice of protecting our digital lives—including our personal information, computers, and networks—from being stolen, damaged, or accessed by unauthorized people.
questions.hint: Think about why we put locks on our front doors, but apply that to a computer.

questions.question: You receive an email from a person you don't know asking for your home address to send you a 'free prize.' What is the safest action to take?
options: Forward the email to all your friends so they can win too
Delete the email and do not share any personal information
Send them your address so you don't miss out on the prize
Reply and ask for more details about their company first
questions.explanation: Sharing personal information like your home address with strangers online is a major privacy risk. Scammers often use 'free prizes' as bait to collect data for identity theft.
questions.hint: If something sounds too good to be true from a stranger, it usually is.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes your 'digital footprint'?
options: The amount of electricity used by your electronic devices
The record of everything you do, post, or leave behind online
The physical size of your computer or smartphone
A special password used to unlock a digital device
questions.explanation: Your digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind on the internet. This includes social media posts, comments, and websites you visit. It can be permanent and seen by others.
questions.hint: Think about the trail of tracks you leave behind when walking on a beach.

questions.question: While browsing a website, a pop-up appears saying your computer is infected with viruses and tells you to 'Click here to clean.' What is this most likely?
options: An automatic update for your internet browser
A helpful warning from your computer's manufacturer
A sign that you need to buy a new computer immediately
A common online threat designed to trick you into clicking a bad link
questions.explanation: Scary pop-ups are often 'scareware'—a type of threat designed to trick you into downloading real viruses or giving away information. Legitimate security software does not use random web pop-ups to warn you.
questions.hint: Real security programs don't usually use bright, flashing advertisements to help you.

questions.question: What does it mean to be a good 'digital citizen'?
options: Knowing how to bypass security to see other people's accounts
Spending at least 10 hours a day using digital devices
Having the highest number of followers on a social media platform
Using technology and the internet in a responsible and respectful way
questions.explanation: Digital citizenship is about being safe, respectful, and responsible online. This includes protecting your own privacy and treating others with kindness in digital spaces.
questions.hint: It is very similar to being a good neighbor or student, but in the virtual world.

questions.question: You are creating a new password for your online banking account. Which of the following would be considered the strongest and most secure password?
options: password123
Blue-Octopus-Rain-99!
Qwerty!
Admin2024
questions.explanation: A long passphrase that combines multiple unrelated words with numbers and symbols is much harder for hackers to guess or crack compared to common words or short sequences.
questions.hint: Think about which option is the longest and contains the most variety of character types.

questions.question: Why is it considered dangerous to use the same password for your email, social media, and bank accounts?
options: It takes longer to type the same password multiple times.
It makes the password easier to remember.
Websites will automatically delete accounts with duplicate passwords.
If one account is breached, a hacker can access all your other accounts.
questions.explanation: This practice is called 'credential stuffing.' If a hacker steals your password from a low-security site, they will immediately try that same password on more sensitive sites like your email or bank.
questions.hint: Think about the risk involved if a single 'key' opens every door you own.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of using a Password Manager?
options: To share your passwords with friends and family easily.
To automatically change your passwords every single day.
To help you remember one master password while it stores and encrypts many unique, complex passwords.
To bypass the need for any passwords on your favorite websites.
questions.explanation: Password managers securely store your login information so you can use unique, complex passwords for every site without having to memorize them all.
questions.hint: Focus on the tool's ability to act as a secure 'vault' for all your different login credentials.

questions.question: You log into your account and are prompted to enter a 6-digit code sent to your phone via SMS. What is this security measure called?
options: Biometric Scanning
Password Recovery
Phishing
Two-Factor Authentication (2FA)
questions.explanation: Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) adds a second layer of security. Even if a hacker knows your password, they cannot access your account without the second 'factor' (the code from your phone).
questions.hint: This term refers to needing two different pieces of evidence to prove who you are.

questions.question: You receive an urgent email from 'Technical Support' claiming your account is locked and asking you to reply with your password to verify your identity. What should you do?
options: Delete the email or report it as phishing, as legitimate companies will never ask for your password.
Send a hint to your password instead of the full password.
Change your password to something simple then send it to them.
Reply immediately so you don't lose access to your account.
questions.explanation: Legitimate service providers will never ask for your password via email or phone. This is a common tactic used by scammers to steal credentials.
questions.hint: Real companies have systems to verify you without ever needing to see your actual password.

questions.question: Which of the following is a secure way to keep track of your passwords if you find them hard to remember?
options: Saving them in a plain text file on your desktop named 'Passwords.txt'.
Using a reputable, encrypted digital password manager.
Using your pet's name followed by your birth year for every account.
Writing them on a sticky note attached to your monitor.
questions.explanation: An encrypted password manager is the only secure option listed. Physical notes can be seen by others, and plain text files can be easily read if your computer is compromised.
questions.hint: Look for the option that uses 'encryption' to hide the information from prying eyes.
